teaser: For founders who have already won: the investor buys the founder's shares, the founder lends the company what it needs, and open source keeps everyone honest.
core_idea: A founder with a working, profitable product and competing investors can sell existing shares instead of issuing new ones, so the founder is paid and no control changes hands, then lend part of the proceeds back as a subordinated loan; open source replaces control rights as the investor's protection, because a fork gets the position but not the velocity; the costs are real: no EIS on bought shares, a signalling problem, a creditor conflict, and tax and articles fine print.

the fork disciplines the founder because it is possible, and protects the founder because it is slow.
no part of the money buys the steering wheel

figures.caption: The two-part model: the investor buys the founder's ordinary shares and pays the founder; the founder lends part of the proceeds to the company as a subordinated loan; the company gets cash without new shares; and the investor's protection is the open-source fork, not a board seat.

The same £2 million, two ways, for a UK company worth £10 million: the founder keeps 80% either way; a standard round gives the investor new preferred shares, rights and control, and puts £2 million into the company; selling and lending gives the investor ordinary shares and the fork as protection, and leaves the founder about £1.58 million after tax, to lend back as much as the company needs; and bought shares carry no EIS relief.
